description:
Moonpossible is a 3-person team at NASA Space Apps Haifa 2026 (Technion), working on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. 

We bring experience in software engineering, cloud, DevSecOps, AI and management. 
Interests: the Moon, space exploration, web development and data. Team already formed.
summary: Other tools show where the Sun and Earth are; Moonpossible makes the landing decision. At the Moon's south pole a lander needs sunlight for power and a direct radio line to Earth, but the Sun skims the horizon at about 2 degrees, so terrain can hide it for days, and launch dates slip often. Moonpossible is an interactive map of the south pole: you choose a mission (crewed or robotic), tap a known site or any point near the pole, pick a date, and get a verdict (passes anywhere, precision landing only, or fails, with the reason), the hours of sunlight and Earth contact, the best dates of the year, and what changes if the launch slips. A landing-windows heatmap colours the whole polar area by where a landing works on a chosen date. Because a lander cannot hit an exact point, we check 9 points across the 100 m landing circle: in our example, landing 100 m off target drops Earth contact from 100% to 39%, and a one-week slip puts the same site into 114 hours of darkness. Every number is computed from NASA and JPL data (LOLA terrain from LRO, JPL SPICE) and validated against JPL Horizons and NASA reference products.
details:
What it does:
Moonpossible is a web app that turns Sun, Earth and terrain geometry at the lunar south pole into a landing decision. The user picks a mission profile (crewed, 156 h stay, or robotic, 14 days), a catalog site or any point within about 51 km of the pole, and a date.
The app answers: can you land here, why or why not, how many hours of sunlight and Earth contact the stay gets, which dates of the year work best, and what changes if the launch slips by N days.

How it works:
For every hour of the stay we compute the Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation with JPL SPICE, and compare them with a terrain horizon built from NASA LOLA elevation models in 720 directions, out to 200 km. Because a lander cannot hit an exact point, we repeat this for the target and 8 points on the 100 m landing circle. The result is one of three verdicts: passes anywhere, passes only at the target point (precision landing needed), or fails with the reason. Landing slope is measured over a 100 m baseline. Every rule is labelled as a NASA-sourced value or a team assumption.

Main features
Basic mode gives a plain sentence and two meters, Power and Contact. Advanced mode adds a yearly calendar of the best site per day, a date range, the 9 landing points, a horizon panorama with playback of the stay, one-click launch slip, a flat-versus-terrain comparison, and a landing-windows heatmap of the whole polar area with filters and preferences.

Example
At Connecting Ridge on 16 December 2026 the target point has 100% sunlight and Earth contact, but 100 m away Earth contact drops to 39%. If the launch slips one week, sunlight at the target drops to 26.7% with 114 hours of darkness, and the site fails. With a flat horizon the same week would look perfect.

Validation
A Validation page compares our results with independent NASA sources: Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons within 0.052 arcseconds, our sunlit and Earth-visible rule matches Horizons on 2,928 of 2,928 samples (geometric horizon, no terrain), and at the IM-1 Odysseus landing point we compute a 12.6 degree slope against about 12 degrees reported by NASA. Checks that only partly match are shown as partial, with the reason.

Tools
Python with SpiceyPy and NumPy, FastAPI, Next.js with TypeScript, OpenLayers and three.js, hosted on Vercel and Supabase Storage.

Goal
Give mission planners a new answer in seconds instead of hours when a schedule slips, and help educators and the public see why the south pole is hard.
dataRefs: NASA GSFC PGDA - LOLA south pole digital elevation models (LRO)
NASA GSFC PGDA - lunar polar illumination and Earth visibility (product 69)
NASA JPL NAIF - SPICE toolkit and kernels
NASA JPL Horizons - ephemerides used for validation
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio - lunar south pole visualization (SVS 5127)
